Article Title: Apple may launch its first touch-screen MacBook on October 27: Report
Article Text:
Apple may launch its first touch-screen MacBook on October 27

What to expect from Apple’s rumoured October 27 event

Apple announces ‘Welcome home’ event for October 13

Apple is planning to introduce its first MacBook with touch screen on October 27, reports Bloomberg citing people with knowledge of the matter. The end-of-month announcements will also include versions of the 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac with M6 chips, said the source cited by the publication. As per the report, the company may also bring a new iPad mini at the event. The reported October 27 event will follow the October 13 event where the company will unveil its revamped smart home strategy. Like its smart home event on October 13, the next launch will include an online video presentation and in-person component for the press, the report says.As stated in the Bloomberg report, the company will debut both MacBooks and iPad later this month. The new lineup, it says, “will be geared toward creative professionals who work in video production, photo editing and music production”.Further, the unveilings are said to be part of a record-setting slate of fresh products under new CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook last month. Tetanus is reportedly aiming to steer the tech giant into new markets and bolster revenue from related services.Meanwhile, the company has announced a ‘Welcome home’ event for October 13.Apple’s SVP of Worldwide Marketing, Greg Joswiak posted a teaser video of the launch on X. The company is expected to unveil its “long-awaited smart home hub with a screen, the new HomePod mini and an updated Apple TV.The most notable launch is expected to be a new smart home hub with a built-in display, which could compete with devices such as Google Nest Hub and Amazon Echo Show. The device is rumoured to feature an S11 chip, which could support faster performance and Siri AI features. The screen could be used to show information such as weather updates, calendar events and music controls.A FaceTime camera is also among the expected features, potentially allowing the device to double as a video-calling hub. Apple is also reportedly developing a specialised operating system for the device focused on smart home controls.
Article Summary: Apple is planning to introduce its first MacBook with touch screen on October 27, reports Bloomberg citing people with knowledge of the matter. The end-of- month announcements will also include versions of the 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac with M6 chips, said the source cited by the publication. The reported October 27 event will follow the October 13 event where the company will unveil its revamped smart home strategy.

Article Title: Meet Caden Terence Pohlkamp, a teenager from Texas, who built an aquatic robot to save fish and other aquatic life in ponds across the State
Article Text:
What Caden’s aquatic robot found in Texas ponds

From an underwater rover to local environmental research

A Texas teenager has built an aquatic robot to help save fish. Caden Terence Pohlkamp, currently a middle school student, used robotics to study retention ponds and how well they support aquatic life. In coastal Texas communities, retention ponds are important systems for managing stormwater and reducing flood risks. But these man-made reservoirs can also become habitats for fish and other aquatic creatures. Balancing their role in flood management with their ability to support wildlife is not always straightforward. Caden, who is a 7th-grader from Friendswood, decided to investigate the issue himself.According to the Society for Science, Caden wanted to find out if there was an “optimal way to design them to provide suitable habitats for the local marine life.” To do that, he engineered an aquatic remote-operated vehicle that could travel underwater and collect samples without disturbing the ponds.The project combined his interest in marine biology and robotics. Instead of manually entering the ponds or relying only on surface observations, Caden’s submersible data-gatherer let him collect water samples from the bottom of 12 ponds across his town.This approach gave him comparable data across different retention ponds and helped him examine the conditions aquatic animals need to survive.After collecting samples, Caden analysed the water for factors that can affect aquatic life. His research focused on pH levels, turbidity (how cloudy the water is), and dissolved oxygen.The results showed that some design features made retention ponds more suitable for aquatic life. The healthier ponds had between 15% and 30% non-grass vegetation along their edges and also contained fountains. These ponds recorded higher levels of dissolved oxygen, an important factor for fish and other aquatic organisms.Caden learned that plants and trees along the edges could provide habitat for fish and help prevent algae blooms. Excessive algae can remove oxygen from the water, creating more difficult conditions for aquatic life.Caden did not stop after collecting and analysing the samples. He presented his findings to local officials, giving them information that could help identify retention ponds where changes might improve conditions for aquatic life.His project shows how a relatively small robotics experiment can help study an environmental issue in a local community. The aquatic robot allowed Caden to gather information from places that would have been difficult to study consistently without an underwater vehicle.The project also reflects the connection between infrastructure and wildlife in growing coastal communities. Retention ponds are built primarily for stormwater management, but their design can influence whether they also become useful habitats for fish and other organisms.For Caden, the experiment has also connected two interests that could shape his future. By combining robotics with marine biology, the 7th-grader has already begun exploring how technology can help us understand and protect aquatic ecosystems. His underwater rover may have started as a school project, but the data it collected gave him a practical way to study the ponds in his own community.
Article Summary: Caden Terence Pohlkamp, currently a middle school student, used robotics to study retention ponds and how well they support aquatic life. In coastal Texas communities, retention ponds are important systems for managing stormwater and reducing flood risks. Balancing their role in flood management with their ability to support wildlife is not always straightforward.

Article Title: Anthropic is updating its Claude usage policy for the first time after almost a year, may start 'banning' users who ...
Article Text:
What new policy says on abusive behavior towards Claude

Consolidated rules under new sections, clarifying weapons prohibition and more

Anthropic makes ‘not without humans’ guideline clear for Claude

AI giant Anthropic has implemented updates to its acceptable usage policy for the first time in over a year. The changes announced aim to establish strict guardrails against emerging threats such as weaponization, illicit surveillance, and election manipulation, while introducing a unique provision that shields its AI model Claude, from user cruelty.The most unconventional addition explicitly prohibits "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" directed at the AI model itself. Building on an initiative announced last August that permitted Claude to sever interactions with persistently abusive individuals as part of ongoing "model welfare" research. The company confirmed that conversation termination remains its primary remedy. While Anthropic has not clarified whether bad actors might face permanent account bans.Here's what Anthropic policy on banning abusive behaviour towards Claude says, "We’ve added a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models. The policy update is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose. It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research.It adds, "This addition aligns with a step we've already taken, allowing Claude models to end rare conversations with persistently abusive users on Claude.ai and Claude Code. Such abuse is the main focus of this update; Claude’s ability to end these interactions will remain the primary enforcement mechanism."At the same time, the revision sharply targets high-stakes public concerns surrounding deceptive influence operations. Anthropic consolidated several disparate rules into a unified prohibition against covert commercial or political campaigns, explicitly outlawing the use of fake accounts and synthetic amplification to hide who is generating content. The framework also clamps down on election interference, outlawing candidate impersonation, voting misinformation, and coordinated attempts to suppress turnout.Heightened safeguards around military hardware and digital tracking form another pillar of the update. Although Anthropic has long prohibited direct weapons development, company notes in its updated policy that bad actors have repeatedly attempted to harness Claude for targeting guidance and control systems. Consequently, the expanded rules now explicitly bar the creation of operational components for weaponry, including the arming of aerial drones and autonomous platforms.The move reportedly follows findings from the company’s internal threat intelligence reports showing that malicious actors were increasingly attempting to leverage Claude to identify and hunt political dissidents. Under the clarified surveillance ban, any nonconsensual tracking -- whether in real time or through historical data mining -- is strictly forbidden. The system is likewise barred from being used to build surveillance infrastructure or make determinations regarding criminal investigations, arrests, and charging decisions, though Anthropic noted that specific government contracts may permit customized exceptions if appropriate safeguards are established.Anticipating the rapid convergence of artificial intelligence and physical robotics, the policy also introduces mandatory human oversight whenever Claude is integrated with real-world machinery. If the AI is connected to autonomous physical hardware capable of causing bodily injury, a qualified operator must maintain constant visibility and possess the immediate authority to halt operations, setting a cautious baseline as the industry pushes deeper into embodied AI and industrial automation.
Article Summary: Anthropic announces updates to its acceptable usage policy for the first time in over a year. Changes aim to establish strict guardrails against emerging threats such as weaponization, illicit surveillance, and election manipulation. The most unconventional addition explicitly prohibits "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" directed at the AI model itself.

Article Title: A rare Canadian computer was forgotten in an Edmonton barn for decades; its first known unboxing came nearly 45 years after it was built
Article Text:
Image Credit: Carleton University

Importance of the rare Canadian computer discovery in an Edmonton barn

What made AES Data an important name in Canadian computing

How much is known about the Alphaplus 12 today

A forgotten machine returns to Canada's computing history

A rare Canadian-built computer that spent decades forgotten in a rural barn near Edmonton is preparing for a unique second chapter. The AES Alphaplus 12, believed to have been built around 1981, had resurfaced in its original shipping box and was taken to Carleton University in Ottawa for a scheduled public unboxing. The machine has attracted attention because so little documentation exists about this particular model, leaving its internal components and configuration uncertain. Its discovery offered a rare opportunity to examine a little-known part of Canada's early computing history.The rediscovery of the AES Alphaplus 12 is significant not simply because an old machine survived for decades, but because so little is known about the exact model. According to Carleton University's School of Computer Science, the computer remained untouched after its time at the Northern Alberta Institute of Technology (NAIT) before being forgotten in a rural Edmonton barn.The university's announcement, published on 2 September 2026, described the machine as a rare example of Canadian computing heritage. The 2 October unboxing event was scheduled to give specialists an opportunity to identify and assess the machine, and also to establish what can be learned from the surviving hardware.The university also noted that the machine was sealed in its dusty shipping box. That condition made the discovery particularly intriguing, as its contents had not yet been examined in the context of the planned public unboxing.The story of the Alphaplus 12 is closely connected to the development of electronic word processing in Canada. Carleton University's background article identifies Montreal-based AES Data Ltd. as the company behind the machine and traces its design lineage to the earlier AES-90.The AES-90 was an important development because it used a screen to display and edit text electronically. According to Carleton, it introduced capabilities such as automatic line wrapping, text justification and numerical alignment at a time when these functions were far from standard. In 1972, the press described the machine as an electronic editor, reflecting how different it was from conventional typing equipment.By 1978, AES was competing directly with IBM as Canada's largest word-processing supplier, according to the university's account. The company was acquired by Ottawa's Kinburn Technology Corporation in 1987, creating a further connection between its history and the city where the newly recovered machine was taken.Despite AES Data's importance in the word-processing industry, information about the Alphaplus 12 itself remains remarkably scarce. Carleton's School of Computer Science reported finding only 2 pieces of documentation relating specifically to the model. A listing in a British museum archive and a brief reference in a Canadian trade magazine from 1981.Even Ingenium, Canada's national science and technology museum, has early AES word processors and software in its collection but no record of this particular model, the university reported. That gap made the recovered machine especially valuable to researchers trying to establish a clearer picture of the country's computing history.A separate entry in the Time-Line Computer Archive provides some context about the wider Alphaplus family. Its listing for the AES Alphaplus 14 describes a word processor built in the early 1980s by the Montreal-based company. The archive explains that the machine was designed for word processing rather than as a general-purpose computer and features a printer built into the monitor.However, the archive documents the Alphaplus 14, not the recovered Alphaplus 12. Its description therefore offers background on related equipment, rather than proof of the exact features or configuration of the barn discovery.The unboxing at Carleton University took place on 2nd October at 2 pm in room 4155 of the Herzberg Building where a livestream was also planned, according to the university's announcement on 18 September 2026.Carleton's announcement places the discovery within a wider pattern of vintage-computing finds. The university's background article recalls the appearance of roughly 2,200 NABU computers from a barn in Massachusetts in 2023. Those machines had their own Canadian connection, having been developed by the Ottawa-based NABU Network in the early 1980s. It also describes the discovery of two Q1 microcomputers beneath boxes at Kingston University in London.The Alphaplus 12 is a smaller discovery in scale, but its limited documentation made it a unique find in its own right. Its journey from an educational institution in Alberta to decades of obscurity in a barn had left important details about the machine unresolved.
Article Summary: AES Alphaplus 12, believed to have been built around 1981, resurfaced in its original shipping box and was taken to Carleton University in Ottawa for a scheduled public unboxing. The machine has attracted attention because so little documentation exists about this particular model, leaving its internal components and configuration uncertain.

Article Title: Prince William's charitable foundation funded homes on Duchy land in Cornwall; in August, the first phase was handed to a charity, providing accommodation and support for 16 people facing homelessness
Article Text:
As the first residents prepare to move in, the project represents the Duchy of Cornwall’s first housing development specifically designed to address homelessness.

A new beginning in Nansledan

Housing with support at its core

Designed for a lower-carbon future

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of the Nansledan project do you find most important? Sustainable building materials Long-term stability for residents 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A wider community taking shape

A new housing project in Cornwall is putting a different face on the fight against homelessness. Rather than treating shelter as a temporary stopgap, the development in Nansledan, Newquay, combines carefully designed homes with practical support, creating a more secure route towards independent living for people who have experienced homelessness. Scroll down to read the details.According to the Nansledan website, on August 4, 2026, St Petrocs received the keys to the first phase of the development from the Duchy of Cornwall. Funded by The Duke of Cornwall’s Charitable Foundation and built on Duchy-owned land, the scheme will provide accommodation for 16 people across two four-bedroom homes and eight one-bedroom apartments.Built by CG Fry & Son, the development was designed around more than simply providing a roof. On-site counselling space will allow St Petrocs to offer residents support alongside their accommodation, helping them establish greater stability as they work towards securing permanent housing, adds the report. The handover marks the completion of the construction phase and the beginning of the homes’ next chapter, with residents set to move into fully equipped properties, the report adds.The project forms part of Homewards, The Royal Foundation’s five-year programme established by The Duke of Cornwall with the ambition of demonstrating that homelessness can be prevented and made rare, brief and unrepeated.The programme brought the Duchy together with homelessness prevention specialists and people with lived experience, helping shape the design and approach to the development. The result is a model that places housing, wellbeing and community connection on the same footing.For St Petrocs, which supports people experiencing homelessness in Cornwall, the homes offer a chance to provide continuity rather than short-term intervention. Residents will have access to personalised support while becoming part of the wider Nansledan community.As per the report, sustainability is another defining feature of the project. The all-electric homes have been constructed with a focus on reducing both embodied carbon and the emissions associated with everyday use. Ultra-low-carbon cement and blockwork, super-insulated hemp-filled wall panels and solar panels form part of the environmental strategy. The approach is intended not only to reduce the development’s impact but also to keep future running costs lower for St Petrocs.The homes have also been furnished through the Homewards Furniture Project, with support from retailers and partners including Howdens, IKEA, DFS, B&Q, Bosch Home Appliances and Gordon Brown’s The Multibank charity. Sofas, tables, chairs, white goods and fitted kitchens mean residents can move into spaces that are ready to live in from day one.Nansledan itself reflects the Duchy’s broader approach to sustainable development. The urban extension to Newquay combines homes with shops, businesses, community facilities, green spaces and walkable neighbourhoods. The supported housing scheme adds another dimension to that vision: ensuring that those at risk of being left on the margins can also find a place within a growing community.As the first residents prepare to move in, the project represents the Duchy of Cornwall’s first housing development specifically designed to address homelessness. Its significance lies not just in the number of homes created, but in the idea behind them: that secure accommodation, meaningful support and a sense of belonging can work together to help people rebuild their lives.Images Courtesy: BBC and Royal Foundation
Article Summary: Nansledan, Newquay, is the Duchy of Cornwall’s first housing development specifically designed to address homelessness. The scheme will provide accommodation for 16 people across two four-bedroom homes and eight one-bedroom apartments. On-site counselling space will allow St Petrocs to offer residents support alongside their accommodation.

Article Title: Greece is turning a former coal mine into a giant renewable-energy battery; the Kardia project will use the mine’s bottom as a water reservoir to generate 320 MW
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

How is Greece turning former coal mines into renewable energy sites

How will the Kardia mine store electricity for 8 hours

Greece expands battery storage to support its growing solar capacity

How will the South Field mine provide 240 MW of energy storage

Greece is repurposing former lignite mining land in Western Macedonia as part of a renewable energy and storage programme. PPC Group has completed 2,130 MW of photovoltaic projects in Amyntaio and Ptolemaida, with the plants expected to generate 3,150 GWh each year.The company is developing storage facilities that will hold surplus renewable electricity and release it when demand rises. One project at the Kardia mine will use the bottom of the inactive mine as a lower reservoir for a pumped storage system. The facility is designed to have a generation capacity of 320 MW and operate for 8 hours. The programme combines solar generation, battery storage and pumped hydro projects across former mining areas in Northern Greece.PPC Group has completed photovoltaic projects with a total capacity of 2,130 MW in Western Macedonia, using former lignite mine areas in Amyntaio and Ptolemaida. The projects are capable of generating 3,150 GWh, corresponding to nearly 6% of the country’s electricity consumption and meeting the annual needs of approximately 750,000 households.Their operation will prevent more than 1.5 million tons of CO₂ emissions annually.Major projects include the 550 MW ‘Phoebe’ photovoltaic plant near Pontokomi, the 940 MW Amyntaio photovoltaic complex, developed in cooperation with RWE, the 200 MW ‘Helios Velos 1’ plant near Ptolemaida, and the 80 MW ‘Exochi 7’ and ‘Akrini’ plants. Ten smaller photovoltaic stations in former lignite areas will also generate solar energy for thousands of households.The Kardia pumped storage project is being developed in a former mining area after the cooling towers of the units were decommissioned. PPC Group has secured regulatory approvals for the project, which will use the bottom of the former mine as the lower reservoir.It will have a generation capacity of 320 MW for 8 hours. Electricity generated during low-demand periods is used to pump water from the lower reservoir to an upper reservoir, where it is stored as potential energy. When demand increases, the water can flow back down through hydroelectric turbines to generate electricity.The Kardia project is part of a storage programme in Western Macedonia. PPC Renewables has completed two electrochemical energy storage stations in Ptolemaida, near Kardia Power Plant, and Meliti, near Meliti Power Plant. Together, the stations have an installed capacity of 98 MW and storage capacity of 196 MWh.Near the Amyntaio Power Plant, a battery energy storage station is under construction, with a capacity of 50 MW and 200 MWh. It is designed to supply electricity to the grid for up to four hours and is expected to be completed in the coming months. The storage systems will support the integration of photovoltaic plants by absorbing surplus generated energy and releasing it when electricity demand exceeds renewable energy generation.Alongside the Kardia project, PPC Group is advancing a pumped storage unit in the South Field mine. The project is planned with a capacity of 240 MW for 12 hours and costs €310 million. Both pumped-hydro projects are based in former mining areas and have secured regulatory approvals. PPC describes pumped-hydro storage as an energy storage technology that helps mitigate the intermittency of renewable energy sources and contributes to grid stability.A system has two water reservoirs at different elevations and hydroelectric turbines. During low-demand periods, electricity is used to pump water from the lower reservoir to the upper reservoir. When demand increases, water is released through turbines, generating electricity. The projects repurpose inactive mining sites for storage.
Article Summary: Greece is repurposing former lignite mining land in Western Macedonia as part of a renewable energy and storage programme. PPC Group has completed 2,130 MW of photovoltaic projects in Amyntaio and Ptolemaida, with the plants expected to generate 3,150 GWh each year. The company is developing storage facilities that will hold surplus renewable electricity and release it when demand rises.

Article Title: This tiny Egyptian object was mistaken for a copper awl for a century; researchers now say its six surviving leather coils reveal a 5,300-year-old bow-powered rotary drill
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

Badari artefact reveals early mechanical drilling in ancient Egypt

How the bow drill made ancient Egyptian drilling more efficient

PC: Archaeology News Online Magazine

The clues hidden in a 63-millimetre object

Ancient Egyptian drill reveals a complex mix of metals

Tool wear reveals the hidden technology behind ancient Egyptian craftsmanship

A century-old museum artefact reveals its hidden purpose decades later

A small copper-alloy object in a Cambridge museum spent decades attracting little attention. It is only 63 millimetres long and weighs around 1.5 grams, hardly the sort of artefact that might alter the picture of early Egyptian technology.The piece was excavated from a cemetery at Badari in Upper Egypt about a century ago. Its original description was brief, calling it a small copper awl with a leather thong wound around it. That interpretation largely left the object sitting quietly in a collection. Now, close study of its worn surface and the remains of the leather has led archaeologists to identify it as something more specialised: a rotary drill operated with a bow, dating to the Predynastic period, roughly 5,300 years ago, as reported by Newcastle University.The artefact comes from a period when Egypt was still developing into the society later associated with pharaonic rule. Badari was part of this earlier landscape, when communities were already producing increasingly varied tools and objects from copper, stone, flint and organic materials.The newly identified drill predates the first pharaohs by centuries. It also pushes back the evidence for mechanically assisted rotary drilling in Egypt by a considerable margin.Tomb paintings from the New Kingdom, for instance, show craftsmen using bow drills to work materials such as wood and beads. The earliest known Egyptian depiction of such a tool had previously been dated to the Old Kingdom, around 2450 BCE, in the tomb of the official Ty at Saqqara.The principle behind a bow drill is straightforward, although the effect is more efficient than an ordinary hand tool. A cord is wound around a narrow shaft, with the shaft carrying a pointed working end. The cord is attached to a bow, and moving the bow backwards and forwards makes the shaft spin alternately in opposite directions.That repeated movement allows the tip to rotate quickly without requiring the craftsperson to twist the tool directly by hand. It could be used for making holes in materials including wood, stone and beads. Similar arrangements were also used in some traditions to produce fire through friction.For early craftspeople, the difference would have been practical. A rotating tool could make controlled holes with less effort than an awl being repeatedly pushed or turned by hand. The newly examined object suggests that this principle was already being used in Egypt during the late fourth millennium BCE.Reportedly, the object is catalogued as 1924.948 A in the Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology at the University of Cambridge. Its original excavator had noticed the leather around it, but the description did not identify a complete mechanical system. Closer examination has changed that interpretation.The metal carries fine marks and rounded areas of wear, along with a slight curvature at the working end. Taken together, the researchers say these traces fit repeated rotary movement better than the use of a simple pointed awl.Even more revealing are six surviving coils of an extremely fragile leather thong. The team believes these are remnants of the cord that would have been wrapped around the shaft and attached to a bow.The work was carried out by Dr Martin Odler of Newcastle University and Jiří Kmošek, an archaeometallurgist and PhD candidate at the Academy of Fine Arts, Vienna. Their study was published in Egypt and the Levant The researchers also examined what the drill was made from. Portable X-ray fluorescence analysis showed an unusual composition containing arsenic and nickel, along with significant amounts of lead and silver.The combination raises questions about how early Egyptian metalworkers selected and worked their materials. The researchers suggest that the unusual composition could reflect deliberate choices in alloying or the movement of particular materials and metallurgical knowledge through wider networks in the eastern Mediterranean during the fourth millennium BCE.For years, much of what was known about Egyptian tools came from their shapes, later written descriptions and scenes painted or carved on tomb walls. Those sources are useful, but they do not always reveal how an object was actually used. Wear on a tool can provide a different kind of evidence.That is the approach behind the UKRI-funded EgypToolWear project, which brings together archaeological, technological and scientific methods to study Egyptian metal tools. Rather than treating museum objects simply as examples of known tool types, the project examines physical traces left by use.In this case, that approach has made an object that once looked like an insignificant copper awl considerably more interesting. It also challenges the assumption that early Egyptian toolmaking developed in a slow or straightforward sequence. Mechanical combinations of wood, leather, cord, stone and metal could produce useful machines even when individual components were relatively simple.The drill was excavated roughly a century ago, catalogued and placed in a museum collection. Nothing about its small size suggested that it would become a major piece of evidence for the history of Egyptian technology. Its significance emerged only when its surface and surviving organic material were examined more closely.That is an important feature of archaeological collections. An artefact does not necessarily become more informative because it is newly excavated. Sometimes the change comes from asking a different question of something that has been sitting in a drawer for generations.Here, the leather coils helped connect the metal shaft to a mechanical arrangement, while the wear on the copper-alloy tip provided clues about how that arrangement may have been used. Together, those details support the identification of the object as the earliest known rotary metal drill from ancient Egypt.
Article Summary: The piece was excavated from a cemetery at Badari in Upper Egypt about a century ago. Its original description was brief, calling it a small copper awl with a leather thong wound around it. Now, close study of its worn surface and the remains of the leather has led archaeologists to identify it as a rotary drill operated with a bow.

Article Title: In 2024, Sydney laid a road using fibres from discarded coffee cups and a petroleum-free binder; 15,600 heavy vehicles crossed it in 75 days as tests indicated improved durability
Article Text:
Representative image of a road being paved with recycled coffee-cup fibres and a petroleum-free binder, highlighting a more durable recycled road surface. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

From discarded cups to road-building material

In an innovative trial, Sydney Water tested a new asphalt blend incorporating fibres from discarded coffee cups and a bio-binder.

A thinner road takes on heavy traffic

What the Sydney experiment could mean for future roads

A Sydney road trial has turned waste and renewable materials into a working asphalt surface. In February 2024, workers laid a section of temporary road at Sydney Water’s Upper South Creek Advanced Water Recycling Centre in Kemps Creek using cellulose fibres recovered from discarded coffee cups and a petroleum-free bio-binder.According to Sydney Water , the trial tested whether waste-derived and renewable materials could withstand demanding construction traffic. Over 75 days, more than 15,600 heavy-vehicle movements were recorded across the trial area. The utility later reported that the experimental asphalt appeared to show improved durability and allowed the pavement to be laid thinner than the conventional comparison surface. As road builders look for ways to reduce the environmental impact of conventional asphalt, the Sydney project tested whether waste fibres and renewable materials could perform on roads carrying heavy traffic.Disposable coffee cups are difficult to recycle. Although they are largely made from paper, many have a thin plastic lining that makes conventional recycling more complicated. Research suggests that this fibre-rich material can be recovered and used in asphalt mixtures. A study published in Construction and Building Materials examined shredded coffee cups as a substitute for conventional cellulose fibres used in stone mastic asphalt.The researchers found that small quantities could reduce binder drain-down while maintaining performance comparable to commercial cellulose fibre.The Sydney project used PAKPAVE, a cellulose-fibre product made from waste coffee cups collected through Closed Loop’s Simply Cups program. Sydney Water also notes that each tonne of trial asphalt contained the equivalent of 364 coffee cups. Should the process eventually become a part of the project for permanent internal roads, then the organisation had expected to save up to 415,000 cups from being sent to landfill. The asphalt was also manufactured using SAMIGreen, a polymer-modified, petroleum-free binder containing biogenic materials. This differed from conventional bitumen, which is typically derived from petrochemicals.The trial used stone mastic asphalt containing recycled coffee-cup fibres and bio-binder, laid to a thickness of about 35mm over approximately 295 square metres. This was paired with a traditional pavement construction using around 45mm of asphalt. It was not just a question of economising on the use of materials. Sydney Water tests showed that the recycled fibre and bio-binder mix could produce a more durable pavement, allowing for a thinner layer. Both the trial pavement and the control pavement used 25 tonnes of material.The traffic provided the strongest real-world test. More than 15,600 heavy-vehicle movements took place on the pavement during the 75-day trial. The project initially reported the figure as more than 14,600 movements, which was later revised to more than 15,600. The project reported a 25% reduction in carbon emissions compared with SMA and a 14% reduction compared with dense-graded asphalt. The difference reflected the project's assessment of the materials, pavement thickness and the baseline used for each comparison.The process is attractive because it addresses two problems at once. Hard-to-recycle coffee cups can be used as a fibre, while a part of the oil-based binder can be substituted with a sustainable material. In Sydney, the experiment concerned a temporary road only and is not evidence that all roads can instantly be constructed with the help of coffee-cup fibres and bio-binder. The project says it has not yet been decided whether the mix will be used on permanent roads at the facility.Nevertheless, the test provided something a laboratory could not: real-world traffic from thousands of heavy vehicles. The test showed that pavement made from recycled coffee cups could be manufactured, laid, and tested under heavy construction traffic alongside an asphalt control section. If the materials continue to meet engineering standards, coffee cups may find a new use in Sydney roads.
Article Summary: Sydney Water tested a new asphalt blend incorporating fibres from discarded coffee cups and a bio-binder. Over 75 days, more than 15,600 heavy-vehicle movements were recorded across the trial area. The trial pavement and the control pavement used 25 tonnes of material.

Article Title: In 2016, Michigan paved a school-bus route with recycled tyre rubber; after 3 years, inspectors found no visible cracking or rutting
Article Text:
Representative AI image of workers paving a school-bus route with recycled tyre rubber and tyre tubes. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

A road built with old tyres

What happened after three years?

Davison Elementary School is located at 2800 E Davison St, Detroit. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

Why the experiment mattered

Every school day, buses travelled along a residential road in Davison, Michigan, carrying children to and from school. In 2016, the road became the site of a less conventional experiment: part of its asphalt was made with rubber recovered from discarded tyres. According to the Transportation Research Board , the test was small, but its setting made it useful. The road, Cambridge Drive between S. State and S. Dayton Street, carried the city's school buses twice a day during the school year.It also provided access to an apartment complex and received direct sunlight, exposing the pavement to both regular traffic and Michigan's changing weather. Three years later, researchers inspecting the experimental section found little to complain about. The pavement showed no visible cracking or rutting, while its condition rating remained high. The result offered a practical glimpse into how waste tyres could be given a second life beneath everyday traffic.The material used in Davison was not simply pieces of tyre scattered through the concrete. In the experiment conducted by the researchers, they used pre-conditioned dry-process ground tyre rubber, or DP-GTR.The rubber particles measured between 400 and 600 micrometres in diameter. The study also notes that the Michigan section used a nominal maximum aggregate size of 12.5 mm, 4.9% binder and 10% DP-GTR. Unlike the wet process, where rubber is blended into the bitumen before the asphalt mixture is produced, the dry process introduces the rubber directly into the mixture during production. The rubber becomes part of the aggregate-binder system as the asphalt is mixed, allowing the process to be carried out with only minor changes to conventional asphalt plant equipment.Davison Road was a useful practical test because the mixture had to withstand vehicle traffic rather than laboratory conditions. Researchers examining the road in 2019 found no cracking or rutting in their visual observations. Using the PASER pavement rating method, the Michigan section scored 8.1. The laboratory results were less straightforward. The authors used different laboratory methods to test cracking and rutting resistance in the rubber-modified mixes. Some laboratory cracking tests were less favourable after rubber was added.The field observations helped contextualise those laboratory results. The researchers reported good-to-excellent performance across the field sections in Michigan, Illinois and Georgia, with limited cracking, rutting, and other visible distress. A separate study of crumb-rubber mixtures published in the International Journal of Pavement Research and Technology also found that field sections built in Michigan showed no rutting after five years of service, while some cracking appeared in neighbouring control lanes using conventional bitumen.Old tyres are difficult waste because they are bulky, durable, and hard to dispose of traditionally. Using them as road material helps keep rubber in circulation while reducing the need for some virgin materials. The Michigan study also showed why pilot studies matter: asphalt blends can perform differently in real traffic than in the lab. The 2016 Davison project did not prove that all rubber-modified roads are more durable, and three years was not long enough to assess a pavement's full lifecycle. It was, however, a relatively small pavement test on a low-volume residential road. Still, the lack of cracking or rutting after three years was a positive result.The researchers' 2021 study concluded that pre-treated rubber could improve some high-temperature and rutting-resistance properties of pavements. In Michigan, the goal was less to replace conventional asphalt immediately than to find a useful outlet for a troublesome material. An old tyre that might otherwise have become waste could instead become part of the road that carries schoolchildren each day.
Article Summary: Davison Elementary School is located at 2800 E Davison St, Detroit. Researchers used pre-conditioned dry-process ground tyre rubber, or DP-GTR. The rubber particles measured between 400 and 600 micrometres in diameter. Researchers examining the road in 2019 found no cracking or rutting.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Article Title: Anthropic launches free AI-powered security scanner for open-source software projects
Article Text:
How OSS Scanner from Anthropic works

Anthropic spent several weeks testing

How to join

AI giant Anthropic has introduced a free vulnerability-scanning service for open-source software projects, using its latest Claude models to identify security flaws and generate bug reports as the company expands its efforts to apply artificial intelligence to cybersecurity. The new service, called OSS Scanner, is an opt-in programme that offers periodic security scans to eligible open-source projects at no cost. Anthropic said the initiative draws on lessons from its vulnerability research efforts under Project Glasswing and is designed to help maintainers discover and fix software weaknesses before attackers can exploit them.According to Anthropic, language models have become significantly more capable at finding software vulnerabilities. The company said AI systems have improved from detecting fewer than 20% of vulnerabilities on a key academic benchmark early last year to finding more than 85% this year.OSS Scanner's output is fully model-generated, with no human review or triage. Anthropic said this allows faster and more frequent scans but means some reports may be incorrect or invalid. Each report includes a self-contained reproducer and an explanation of the vulnerability.Where possible it also traces when the bug was introduced, and it offers a candidate patch when one is available.Anthropic will keep sending human-verified reports through its existing coordinated vulnerability disclosure process, especially for projects that lack resources to triage reports themselves. OSS Scanner is an optional fast track for maintainers who want reports as soon as they are generated. It is separate from Claude Security, Anthropic's general-access code scanning and patching product for enterprises.Anthropic spent several weeks testing the pipeline with dozens of open-source projects. The first disclosures contained hundreds of bug reports, including several vulnerabilities that could be chained into unauthenticated remote code execution exploits.In one validation exercise, expert penetration testers who review Anthropic's disclosures checked 97 critical and high-severity findings across 48 projects. Of these, 85 (88%) met the bar for the disclosure process. Of the other 12, 11 were real but duplicated known issues or other scan findings, and one was a false positive. Anthropic acknowledged that some maintainers have said severity ratings can be inflated, or that the scanner misunderstood a project's threat model.Maintainers who tested early versions were largely positive:* PostgreSQL: Noah Misch said several reports came with fixes the project could use nearly as they were, and that fast-track access let the team address new issues before a general-availability release.* OpenSSL Corporation: Anton Arapov said the reports, raw model output included, were as good as and sometimes better than those from people, especially when an exploit was attached.* wolfSSL: Todd Ouska said that of 74 reports, all but two were valid and five became CVEs.* HotCRP: Eddie Kohler praised the reports for their grasp of the project's complex permission model.Core maintainers of eligible projects can enroll by submitting a pull request to a GitHub repository Anthropic has set up. Eligibility follows criteria similar to OSS-Fuzz's, chiefly that a project has "critical impact on infrastructure and user security." Anthropic will decide case by case. Anthropic also pointed to two related programs: a Cyber Verification Program that gives qualifying security professionals advanced cyber capabilities with fewer blocking classifiers, and Claude for OSS, which offers free Claude Max 20x subscriptions to help fix vulnerabilities.
Article Summary: OSS Scanner is an opt-in programme that offers periodic security scans to eligible open-source projects at no cost. Anthropic said the initiative draws on lessons from its vulnerability research efforts under Project Glasswing. Each report includes a self-contained reproducer and an explanation of the vulnerability.

Google Cloud unveiled the Gemini agent at its annual Gemini at Work 2026 conference, positioning the system as a universal, single digital assistant engineered to handle enterprise knowledge work, run complex code and execute multi-step workflows straight from a prompt box. According to Google Cloud, nearly 500 enterprise customers each processed over one trillion tokens in the past year alone. Furthermore, approximately 80% of all Google Cloud clients now deploy its artificial intelligence offerings, while nearly 90% of Fortune 100 enterprises actively use Gemini Enterprise. With business environments pivoting toward agentic systems, Google stated that the new Gemini agent is built around delegating end objectives rather than micromanaging step-by-step instructions.The Gemini agent is designed around six core architectural pillars.Users can chat, delegate autonomous objectives, schedule background duties, and generate code from a consolidated interface without switching between disconnected applications.The system functions across web interfaces, iOS, Android, macOS, and Windows. It integrates directly into developer command lines, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and Slack, or operates headlessly behind third-party enterprise tools.Running entirely on cloud infrastructure, the agent retains a shared memory bank and personalization graph across all endpoints. Users can initiate a job that runs for hours or days, close their computer, and return to completed deliverables without re-briefing the system.When handling complex projects, Gemini can spin up specialised, temporary sub-agents to tackle parallel or sequential tasks. It can also stand up permanent "coworker agents" assigned to specific team functions. These coworker agents receive their own dedicated email addresses (such as @agents.company.com), independent cloud storage, and role boundaries.The system retains four distinct layers of memory: session memory for active jobs; semantic memory for company documentation; procedural memory for repeatable workflows; and episodic memory to recall past interactions.Flexible multi-model routing: The agent decouples the user experience from the underlying foundation model. It dynamically routes queries to the most cost-effective and accurate engine available, navigating Google’s own Gemini family alongside Anthropic’s Claude models, with support for future private and open-source models.The agent works directly across Gmail, Drive, Docs, Slides, Sheets, Chat and Calendar through three primary modes:Knowing a user’s schedule and team relationships, the agent can coordinate across apps automatically. For example, it can assemble an attendee list from past chat threads, review calendars, and send scheduling emails without requiring manual contact entry.Built-in Workspace Intelligence identifies tasks within inbound emails, such as a manager requesting a presentation, and serves up one-click prompts allowing users to delegate the task directly to Gemini. The inbox also highlights messages based on operational importance rather than arrival time.Departments can generate artificial colleagues that show up directly in corporate directories with their own calendar and Drive storage. Team members can tag the coworker agent in Chat or add them to document comments, where the agent suggests edits and answers questions under its own identity without exposing wider personal files.
Article Summary: The Gemini agent is designed around six core architectural pillars. Article Title: Popular VC Paul Graham disagrees with Amazon ‘ban’ on Meta's Muse and Perplexity's Comet AI; says that blocking AI Agents will backfire
Article Text:
Amazon’s pushback against ‘outside’ AI

Renowned venture capitalist and Y Combinator co-founder Paul Graham has criticised Amazon ’s aggressive crackdown on third-party AI shopping assistants, warning that shutting out these automated agents may open the door for a startup rival to challenge the e-commerce giant’s market dominance. In multiple posts shared on X (formerly Twitter), Graham argued that consumer habits are shifting toward agentic workflows, and attempting to lock external tools out of storefronts will inevitably backfire by fueling demand for more open competitors.“Amazon banning agents is the first opportunity I've seen since Amazon was founded for a startup to create an Amazon competitor. People will want agents to buy stuff for them. It will be one of the main use cases. And they won't want to use some Amazon-supplied agent to do it,” Graham said.He framed restrictive platform policies as an open invitation for disruption, adding: “Any business that bans agents represents an opportunity for a startup to create a competitor. If they need to ban agents, it must mean people want to use them, or there would be no point. And that in turn means there's demand for a competitor that allows them.Your usage restrictions are my opportunity.”Graham’s remarks follow a series of defensive moves by Amazon to shield its marketplace from outside AI scrapers and purchasing bots.In September, Amazon confirmed it cut off Meta’s new Muse personal AI agent from shopping on Amazon.com on behalf of users. The retail titan stated that it took the step after trying unsuccessfully to convince Meta to voluntarily leave the e-commerce site out of the experience.Further, Amazon claimed it never permitted the access, noting that Meta failed to give prior notification, that Muse browse sessions do not identify themselves and that the tool appears to capture and store customer credentials, creating potential privacy and security vulnerabilities.Prior to the ban on Meta’s Muse, Amazon was in a year-long effort to block third-party agents across the board. The company filed a lawsuit against AI search firm Perplexity over its Comet browser and moved to prevent shopping agents built by Google and OpenAI from crawling its marketplace.Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, an AI agent that researches products and makes recommendations.
Article Summary: Y Combinator co-founder Paul Graham has criticised Amazon’s aggressive crackdown on third-party AI shopping assistants. Graham argued that shutting out these automated agents may open the door for a startup rival to challenge the e-commerce giant”s market dominance. He framed restrictive platform policies as an open invitation for disruption, adding: “Your usage restrictions are my opportunity”

Article Title: She homeschools four children while running 11 AI agents: How this founder turned her home into an AI laboratory
Article Text:
Jesse Genet's homeschooling agents use OpenClaw

For Jesse Genet, running a household with four young children and homeschooling three of them could easily be a full-time job. Instead, the former Silicon Valley founder is using 11 AI agents to handle parts of her family’s education and everyday household work. Genet, a former Y Combinator founder who previously built and sold a packaging company, said she had expected to step away from technical work for several years so she could focus on her children. That changed after she began experimenting with AI agents that could build and complete tasks for her.“I feel like I've been building better things than I ever have before,” Genet said on the A16Z podcast.Genet's three older children are aged five, four and two, while her fourth child is a baby. She uses AI agents to help prepare lessons based on the homeschooling curricula she follows. Her main homeschooling agent, which she calls Sylvie, has access to the core curriculum texts, Genet's education philosophy and photos of the Montessori materials available at home. It can create lesson plans and suggest which materials to use.Genet also uses voice notes and photos to record what her children learned. An agent turns those quick updates into detailed lesson logs, helping it keep track of where each child is in the curriculum.The AI is not limited to homeschooling. Genet said she uses agents to order groceries, buy items needed for children's activities and handle other household tasks.Jesse Genet said she now has 11 agents, 10 of which use OpenClaw. She runs them on Mac Minis and uses Obsidian to store information and lesson logs. Her setup has also become increasingly autonomous. Genet said her existing agents can now create new agents themselves when they become overloaded with work.She said she wants to use AI whenever she encounters a task that takes her away from what she actually wants to be doing, such as spending time with her children.But the experiment has also shown the risks. Genet once gave an AI agent access to her email. After she mentioned struggling to send an important email, the agent interpreted it as a request for help and sent the message on her behalf. She later removed its ability to send emails.“Trust, but verify,” Genet said, describing the lesson she took from the incident.Genet said the experience reinforced the need to restrict what AI agents are technically allowed to do rather than simply telling them not to do something.
Article Summary: Former Y Combinator founder Jesse Genet is using 11 AI agents to handle parts of her family’s education and everyday household work. Her main homeschooling agent, which she calls Sylvie, has access to the core curriculum texts, Genet's education philosophy and photos of the Montessori materials.

Article Title: Bill Gates secretly credited him as a creator of Windows 1.0; forty years later Gabe Newell three months under him taught him more than his time at Harvard; lesson he has taken to the seas
Article Text:
The Windows 1.0 lesson that traveled to Sea

How Newell brought team philosophy on his superyacht

What makes Leviathan different

Gabe Newell worked under Bill Gates developing the initial version of Windows at Microsoft in his early years. Forty years ago, his name was quietly coded into a hidden screen inside a fledgling operating system that would revolutionise personal computing. Today, the Valve co-founder and gaming billionaire has brought that same ethos of recognising the contributors to his 364-foot, $500 million megayacht, Leviathan.Newell was just 23 years old when Microsoft rolled out Windows 1.0 on November 20, 1985. The MS-DOS-based release faced widespread development delays and industry skepticism, with critics initially brushing it off as “vaporware.” Behind the scenes, a core team of around 13 people was pushed to solve systemic engineering hurdles rather than stay confined to narrow job descriptions. Newell has repeatedly credited this high-intensity phase as the foundation of his managerial style, noting that just three months working under Bill Gates taught him far more than his entire education at Harvard University.That tight-knit software team left a secret calling card. Embedded inside a bitmap file was an unlisted credit roll bearing 36 names, including Newell and Steve Ballmer, which was triggered by an intricate keyboard sequence.As recounted during 40th-anniversary project retrospectives, Gates stumbled across an early iteration of the screen after punching in keys in frustration over system latency, prompting developers to make the trigger even harder to find. The hidden roster stayed undiscovered until 2022, when a security researcher reverse-engineered the original binaries, as reported by PC World.Delivered last year by Dutch shipbuilder Oceanco, the Leviathan vessel stands as an intensely personal creation for Newell. Apart from a 10-meter pool, expansive panoramic windows and a massive 5.3MWh battery system, the vessel features a sea lobby dedicated entirely to the workforce that built it.At the midships entry point, visitors encounter a full-height glass panel engraved with the names of nearly 3,000 people – spanning Oceanco naval architects, specialist craftspeople, project contractors, and crew members. In a nod to gaming culture, an Oceanco-designed Leviathan crest is etched to appear only when viewed from specific angles, an intentional design detail described by Boat International as an "Easter egg. "The main deck of the Leviathan replaces the standard formal dining hall with a communal layout accommodating up to 56 people, allowing guests and crew to eat together. The bridge deck houses a full basketball hoop and a large games room, while the sundeck includes a spa pool and space for beer pong. The oversized kitchen is engineered with modular cooking stations designed to double as an operational training academy for chefs.Beyond hospitality, Leviathan functions as a versatile mobile base for Newell’s wide-ranging ventures across deep-sea exploration, neuroscience, tooling, and artificial intelligence. Through Inkfish, his marine exploration organisation, Newell supplies resources to oceanographic researchers.Other features include an operational diving and ocean research workshop equipped with a laboratory and 3D printing equipment; an interactive gaming studio outfitted for virtual reality and holographic systems; and a soundproofed lower-deck studio that accommodates music gear, including a full drum kit, and serves as an editing bay for audio and video production.
Article Summary: Gabe Newell's $500 million superyacht features a sea lobby dedicated entirely to the workforce that built it. At the midships entry point, visitors encounter a full-height glass panel engraved with the names of nearly 3,000 people. The main deck of the Leviathan replaces the standard formal dining hall with a communal layout accommodating up to 56 people.

Article Title: ATM’s ‘dying technology’ problem may come to trouble data centres, as these engineers may increasingly ‘disappear’
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation

COBOL is running out of people

Replacing COBOL systems is not simple

COBOL skills are becoming more valuable

COBOL may be decades old, but it still powers critical financial infrastructure and 95% of ATM transactions, according to IBM. Now, as the engineers who maintain these systems age out and fewer young developers learn the language, the skills needed to keep this infrastructure running could become scarce.This could also create problems for data centers supporting financial services, where legacy systems still run on COBOL. Banks and businesses may struggle to maintain systems they can't easily replace, and the shortage of skilled engineers has existed for years. It will only get worse as experienced COBOL programmers retire.COBOL was never designed to become such a deeply embedded part of modern infrastructure. Yet 66 years after its creation, financial institutions, businesses, and governments still use it widely.The language has evolved over time. COBOL introduced object-oriented programming in 2002, while IBM has continued developing products around it. A new standard was also released in 2023. But modernising the language does not solve the shortage of people who can maintain decades-old systems.The problem is not new. Computerworld highlighted the ageing COBOL workforce in 2008 and again in 2012.In 2013, ZDNet reported that universities were avoiding teaching COBOL because it had become "uncool."Moving away from COBOL is difficult because financial systems can contain hundreds of millions of lines of code. Simply asking AI to translate that code into a newer language may not be enough.Calvin Smith, in a breakdown by YouTube channel OpenHands, said attempts to use AI agents for such work have not been particularly successful. IBM also pushed back against the idea that modernising COBOL systems is simply a matter of translating code, saying it involves "data architecture redesign, runtime replacement, transaction processing integrity, and hardware-accelerated performance."That complexity makes any transition, gradual or not, risky. In 2018, a major failure occurred when UK bank TSB shifted from one platform to another. Unable to access their accounts, the bank was then fined £48.65 million ($65.86 million) and affected millions of customers.The shrinking pool of COBOL engineers is also creating financial incentives for those with the expertise. Some jobs require several years of experience with the language and can pay between $100,000 and $150,000, with some positions offering more.The bigger question is what happens when even those engineers begin to disappear. Replacing decades of carefully maintained financial infrastructure with newer languages such as Rust would be expensive and carry significant risks.For banks and other organisations, the challenge may therefore be less about whether COBOL is old and more about whether enough people will remain who understand the systems built around it.
Article Summary: COBOL still powers 95% of ATM transactions, according to IBM. As engineers who maintain these systems age out and fewer young developers learn the language, the skills needed to keep this infrastructure running could become scarce. This could also create problems for data centers supporting financial services.

Article Title: Samsung Galaxy Tab S12+ First Impressions
Article Text: At Rs 1,29,999 in India, the Samsung Galaxy Tab S12+ sits firmly in Samsung’s premium tablet lineup, aimed at users who want a large-screen device for work, entertainment, note-taking and creative tasks. The Tab S12+ also marks an interesting change in Samsung’s tablet lineup. After bringing back an 11-inch model with the Galaxy Tab S11 series, Samsung has moved back to a 12.6-inch Plus model with the Tab S12+. The bigger screen gives it more room to work with, while the tablet remains noticeably smaller and lighter than the 14.6-inch Ultra.We got some time with the Galaxy Tab S12+ and our initial experience suggests that Samsung has focused on refining the formula rather than completely changing it. The tablet gets a brighter display, a newer MediaTek Dimensity 9500 processor, an S Pen in the box and support for Samsung’s laptop-like DeX experience.The first thing that stands out about the Galaxy Tab S12+ is its 12.6-inch Dynamic AMOLED 2X display. It supports a 120Hz adaptive refresh rate and Samsung says the panel can reach up to 1,600 nits of peak brightness.The screen also benefits from Samsung’s Vision Booster technology, which adjusts brightness based on the surrounding lighting conditions.During our initial time with the tablet, the display looked bright and sharp, while the larger 12.6-inch panel gives the S12+ plenty of space for watching videos, browsing and working with multiple apps.The design is also quite slim. The Galaxy Tab S12+ measures 5.3mm in thickness and weighs 553 grams, making it considerably easier to handle than the larger Ultra model. Samsung has also given the tablet an IP68 rating for water and dust resistance, which is useful for a device in this price range.Performance is handled by the MediaTek Dimensity 9500 processor, which is also used in the Tab S12 Ultra. Samsung is promising gains in CPU, GPU and AI performance over the previous generation. Based on our early experience, the tablet feels fast and responsive, although the performance improvements are more evolutionary than revolutionary.The Galaxy Tab S12+ also comes with an S Pen, continuing Samsung’s focus on productivity and creativity. Users can take notes, annotate documents, sketch and use the stylus for other everyday tasks.Samsung is also positioning the Tab S12+ as a potential laptop replacement. Its DeX desktop interface, combined with optional keyboard accessories, gives the tablet a more PC-like experience.For now, the Galaxy Tab S12+ looks like a premium tablet that builds on what Samsung already does well. The 12.6-inch AMOLED display, slim design, S Pen support and flagship processor make a strong first impression. But at Rs 1,29,999, the final verdict will depend on how well these features come together in everyday use, particularly battery life, performance under sustained workloads and whether the tablet can genuinely replace a laptop for some users.
Article Summary: The Galaxy Tab S12+ is aimed at users who want a large-screen device for work, entertainment, note-taking and creative tasks. The 12.6-inch AMOLED display, slim design, S Pen support and flagship processor make a strong first impression. But at Rs 1,29,999, the final verdict will depend on how well these features come together.
